sources.title: See inside the Gen Z protests sweeping Europe as dissent grows - The Washington Post
sources.articleText:
See inside the Gen Z protests sweeping Europe as dissent grows
BERLIN — Thousands of Gen Z-led protesters took to the streets across Germany and other European countries on Halloween, joining a growing wave of youth demonstrations over the rising cost of living, increased military spending, the worsening climate crisis and chronic underinvestment in education.
Lead image: Protesters with a French flag sing on the roof of a bus stop in Paris on Saturday during a demonstration against the high cost of living. (Chloe Sharrock/MYOP/For The Washington Post)
A Berlin protester dressed as Lady Justice poses at the Brandenburg Gate. (Ksenia Ivanova/For The Washington Post)
In some of the European Union’s most influential countries — France, Spain, Italy and Germany and others — young people are increasingly challenging political leaders they see as disconnected from their concerns and indifferent to their future.
Across the continent, people are grappling with sluggish economic growth and soaring costs, compounded by the fallout from the U.S. war with Iran.
A protester holding a sign saying "Such violence!" joins the demonstration in Paris on Saturday. (Chloe Sharrock/MYOP/For The Washington Post)
Protesters hold hands in Paris. (Chloe Sharrock/MYOP/For The Washington Post)
These pressures have intensified a broader sense of disillusionment among younger generations, many of whom fear they will be worse off than their parents. Portuguese protests have centered on affordable housing, while those in Italy started after truck drivers and farmers blockaded roads in the south over high fuel prices and then gained traction amid a wider furor over the cost of living.
People march by the Colosseum in Rome on Friday during a nationwide day of strikes and protests. (Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty Images)
France witnessed its third consecutive weekend of nationwide protests, with hundreds of thousands of people taking part in demonstrations across the country after earlier protests spiraled into rioting and looting. The youth-led movement was fueled by mounting frustration over deteriorating public services and underfunded schools — conditions that also have fueled protests in Belgium.
Paris demonstrations featured a mix of protest gear and colorful Halloween costumes. (Chloe Sharrock/MYOP/For The Washington Post)
Riot police patrol the demonstration in Paris. (Chloe Sharrock/MYOP/For The Washington Post)
Germany joined the wider European protest movement over the Halloween weekend, with demonstrations organized by a loose alliance known as “Gen Z regelt,” roughly translating to “Gen Z’s got this.” German organizers said more than 100,000 people had taken part in protests nationwide, according to the German news agency DPA.
Many demonstrators in Berlin said they had been inspired by the protests in France, where people of all ages joined student-led demonstrations.
Aynur Mengi, 28, and Zülal Öztürk, 30, pose for a portrait during a protest in Berlin. (Ksenia Ivanova/For The Washington Post)
In several German cities, Saturday’s demonstrations descended into violence. In Frankfurt, rioters smashed shop windows and threw molotov cocktails at emergency services personnel, according to police statements. In Berlin, a daytime rally near the city’s landmark Brandenburg Gate passed peacefully. A separate demonstration that evening ended in scuffles.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the tabloid newspaper Bild that police had prevented “excesses of violence like those seen in Paris.” He blamed the unrest on “violent left-wing groups and anarchists from the migrant community” but offered no further details or evidence.
Protesters in Berlin hold a sign that reads, "Our future is scarier than our costumes." (Ksenia Ivanova/For The Washington Post)
For many of the young men gathered in Berlin, opposition to the possible reinstatement of military conscription was a central concern. Germany suspended compulsory military service in 2011, but the government has since moved to expand the armed forces and strengthen national defense following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Other Berlin protesters voiced fears about growing social polarization, saying the deepening divisions leave them worried about the world their children might inherit.
“We are the generation that has to think about our future the most,” said Aynur Mengi, 28. “But every day people choose something for our future without considering our opinions.”
A young protester dressed as Jesus at the Halloween demonstration in Paris. (Chloe Sharrock/MYOP/For The Washington Post)
Garance, 26, dresses as Marie Antoinette to criticize the French government in Paris. (Chloe Sharrock/MYOP/For The Washington Post)
Thomas Kinkade, 23, poses for a portrait during the protest in Berlin. (Ksenia Ivanova/For The Washington Post)
Elie, 20, protested alongside his trade union. (Chloe Sharrock/MYOP/For The Washington Post)
Protesters are caught in a cloud of tear gas during Saturday's demonstration in Paris. (Chloe Sharrock/MYOP/For The Washington Post)
Dezirae, 25, came to support the Saturday protest in Berlin. (Ksenia Ivanova/For The Washington Post)
Mary Ilyushina, a reporter on the Foreign Desk of The Washington Post, covers Russia and the region. She began her career in independent Russian media before joining CNN’s Moscow bureau as a field producer in 2017. She has been with The Post since 2021. She speaks Russian, English, Ukrainian and Arabic.@maryilyushina
